claims.text: The military branch was led from 'one of the central military research institutes in the Moscow region', with its chief V. Balashov as scientific head and a working group of four to five people; roughly fifteen further Ministry of Defence and war-industry organisations participated voluntarily. The academic branch was headed by Academician V. Migulin, director of IZMIRAN, which was 'determined as the head institute in this field of activity', with a working group of four to five headed by Yu. Platov.

claims.text: Two topics were entered in the 1978 defence research plan, verbatim: '"Setka MO" (Ministry of Defence) - "Research of paranormal atmospheric and space phenomena and their influence on the operation of military technical equipment and personnel"; "Setka AS" (Academy of Sciences) - "Research of a physical nature and mechanisms of paranormal atmospheric and space phenomena".'

claims.text: Across the whole programme there was no message about a UFO landing, no message about contact with UFO occupants, and no message about abductions. The authors state the conclusion as a fork: 'either the territory of the USSR was, due to any reasons, closed for alien visitations during, at least, 13 years or that the hypothesis of an extraterrestrial origin of "UFO" is inconsistent.'

claims.text: The research was classified for three stated reasons: it formally entered the classified defence plan; a military-technical origin for the effects was thought likely at the outset; and there was 'a capability of a military use of some probable properties of the UFO ... absence of a radar contrast, high manoeuvrability, etc.' In official documents 'the use of an abbreviation "UFO" was not accepted, instead of it the term "paranormal phenomenon" was used.'

claims.text: Verbatim: 'One can say that the noted directive for 13 years put the army into the on-duty regime of observation of the paranormal phenomena in the places of the army dislocation, i.e. practically on the whole territory of the USSR, and this means, anyway, approximately 1/6 of the Earth territory.' Each serviceman 'became (without knowing it) a potential participant of the program'.

claims.text: 'The budget financing of the research program included the salary of the experts occupied in these activities and the costs of business trips. All the money was coming from the budget of organisations - executors and there was no special financing of the research.' The programme was 'the most inexpensive one, if not the cheapest, among the scientific works on defensive subjects'.

claims.text: 'During the work on the program (for 13 years) about three thousand of messages reporting about extraordinary phenomena have been obtained ... on the whole, more than 400 events were registered and identified as extraordinary or paranormal.' Over 90% were resolved as rocket-launch effects or high-altitude balloons, the balloon class accounting for 10-12% of messages. The Petrozavodsk phenomenon itself was attributed to 'the launch of an artificial Earth satellite "Kosmos 955" from the space range in Plesetsk'. Reports 'did not practically come' from units at or near test ranges, where such effects were familiar.

Migulin, director of IZMIRAN and a radio physicist specialising in oscillation theory, radio wave propagation and radiolocation, was made scientific head of the academic branch, and IZMIRAN was designated head institute. The four-to-five person working group there was headed by Yu. Platov, co-author of the programme's published account.

b.label: United States Department of Defense (secondary designation: Department of War)

edges.label: opposite reporting posture: mandated versus stigmatised
edges.note: A January 1980 Directive of the Soviet General Staff obliged every serviceman to report any inexplicable phenomenon in writing and routed the results to a single analysis centre, putting the army 'into the on-duty regime of observation' for thirteen years. The contrast with the US chain of command over the same period, where reporting carried career risk and no service-wide collection mandate existed, is the comparison this node exists to make. The Soviet side of the comparison is documented by the programme's own coordinators; no institutional contact between the two is claimed.
